newsitem.title: UK: Smith&Nephew says no foundation in bid rumour.
newsitem.headline: Smith&Nephew says no foundation in bid rumour.

text.p: Smith & Nephew's chief executive John Robison said during a telephone conference that he was surprised the healthcare company had recently again become subject of takeover speculation and added the rumours lacked every foundation.
"There is no basis at all for these rumours," he said.
Robinson said Smith & Nephew was not interested in mergers as it was already one of the leading players in the world healthcare market.

Instead, Smith & Nephew is keen to boost its position in the consolidating healthcare industry through acquisitions. With a gearing of just eight percent, Smith & Nephew could spend well over 500 million stg without using equity, Robinson said.

Germany, where Smith & Nephew's presence is not very strong, would be an obvious choice for acquisitions. But the problem here was that were far fewer buying opportunities than in the dynamic U.S. market, Robinson added.
Smith & Nephew expects to see consolidation in the orthopaedic sector and Robinson said: "we could well participate in that over the next year or two."
"But also, care management is another area where we're actually very strong, but there are many operations are going to consolidate in the future," he added.
Smith & Nephew earlier reported a small increase in 1996 pre-tax profit to 182.2 million stg from 180.4 million as market conditions remained tough, particularly in the U.S.

Speaking of the overall results, Robinson said: "In the really quite diffcult market conditions that we were in last year, these are good results relative to the way our competitors have been performing."
Mergers among hospitals and the formation of healthcare buying groups depressed selling prices in the U.S.
"More professional buying by the hospitals than used to happen is the main cause (for the tough U.S. market)," Robinson said.
"It is likely to last, although probably not as severe as last year through this year," he added.
The U.S. makes up about 40 percent of group profits.
Smith & Nephew made strong progress in the fast growing Asian market, but at the moment that region generates just over five percent of total profits, Robinson said.
Smith & Nephew said it planned to launch its promising human tissue skin replacement product, Dermagraft, in Britain and the U.S. in the second half of the year.
The launch in continental Europe will be staggered depending on different national regulatory requirements.
"The big event this year will be Dermagraft," said Robinson. "So as we go forward we are in pretty good shape."

Dermagraft will operate in a potential market with an estimated size of 1.5 billion pounds and Rosinson, citing "market observers", said the product should be able to grab a 10 to 12.5 percent market share.
